To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) area requirements for sampling a herbivore species assemblage are consistently above 50%, regardless of the target population size or the analytical grain used to calculate the area requirement; and (2) area requirements are insensitive to habitat quality, the presence of low density species, or to the coarseness or resolution of the land classification systems used to estimate area requirements.

area requirements for sampling a viable population of species assemblage are insensitive to selection unit, habitat quality, the presence of low density species or the coarseness or land classification system.

the area required to represent viable populations of a species assemblage was consistently above 50%, and was insensitive to selection unit sizes, the coarsence of habitat quality, the presence of low density species or the use of different land classification systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the area requirements for viable populations of species.
the question of what is a ‘representative sample’ of biodiversity, and how can we determine what is a representative sample.
the question of whether or not the current conservation targets of 10-15% of land classification unit areas are adequate for representing the biodiversity features of African savanna regions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
area requirements for sampling a viable population of a species or assemblage are unknown, and that the use of a 50% rule of thumb is not supported by the data.

area requirements for sampling species assemblages of African herbivores are not yet known and that the area requirements of species assemblage sampling may not be a function of the area requirements of individual species.
, at least in the case of herbivore assembles, conservation targets for viable assemblages should be at least 50%, but may be considerably higher.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of 10–20% conservation targets is not justified for the Kruger National park.
the area requirements for viable populations of a single species or assemblages of species are likely to be much higher than previously estimated.

the use of a 50% conservation target for African savanna regions is a reasonable rule of thumb, but that the use of this or any other conservation rule of thumb should be abandoned when data on the spatial distribution of biodiversity are available.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single target area to represent the biodiversity of a given area is likely to be inappropriate.
we need to be very careful when we are setting conservation targets.
we need to be careful when using data-independent conservation targets.
